hood_desc: Plateau-Mont-Royal is the quintessential bohemian Montreal neighborhood, packed with colorful triplexes, winding outdoor staircases, indie boutiques and sidewalk cafes. Lively, walkable and largely French-speaking, it suits students, artists and visitors wanting the trendy heart of the city.

Mile End is the citys creative and hipster hub, famous for its wood-fired bagel shops, indie music scene, vintage stores and laid-back cafes. Multicultural and low-key cool, it appeals to foodies, creatives and a younger crowd chasing authentic local flavor.

Vieux-Montreal (Old Montreal) charms with cobblestone streets, centuries-old stone architecture, boutique hotels and waterfront views along the Old Port. Romantic but touristy and pricier, it suits travelers who want history, fine dining and Old World ambiance.

Griffintown is a fast-changing former industrial district near the Lachine Canal, now full of glassy condo towers, modern lofts and buzzy new restaurants. Central and stylish, it draws young professionals wanting an up-and-coming, contemporary vibe.

Outremont is an affluent, leafy francophone enclave of elegant homes, tree-lined streets and upscale bakeries and boutiques. Quiet, refined and family-oriented, it suits those seeking a calm, sophisticated residential setting away from the tourist bustle.

water.note: Tap water is safe and well-regulated; older buildings occasionally have lead pipe concerns.

transit.pay: Buy a reloadable OPUS card for C$6 (~$4.40) at metro station machines/counters or authorized retailers, then load fares and tap to enter. A single fare is about C$3.75 (~$2.75); an unlimited day pass is about C$11.50 (~$8.50). The Chrono app can also load fares onto your phone.
transit.hours: The Metro runs about 5:30am to 1am (later on weekends); an all-night bus network covers the city after the metro closes.

food.name: Poutine
food.desc: Quebec's late-night icon: hot fries topped with squeaky cheese curds and brown gravy, ideally eaten well after midnight.

places.name: La Banquise
places.note: Open 24 hours with more than 30 versions; the classic is still the benchmark.

places.name: Chez Claudette
places.note: Neighbourhood casse-croute locals rate above the tourist spots.

places.name: Ma Poule Mouillee
places.note: Portuguese-Quebecois hybrid topped with grilled chicken and chorizo.

food.name: Montreal bagel
food.desc: Thinner and sweeter than New York's, boiled in honey water and baked in a wood-fired oven. Best eaten hot from the bag with sesame seeds.

places.name: St-Viateur Bagel
places.note: Open 24 hours since 1957; watch them come off the wooden peel.

places.name: Fairmount Bagel
places.note: The other half of the city's oldest rivalry, a block away. Try both.

food.name: Smoked meat sandwich
food.desc: Brisket cured for over a week, smoked and steamed, hand-sliced and stacked on rye with yellow mustard. Order it medium-fat.

places.name: Schwartz's Deli
places.note: The 1928 original on Saint-Laurent; the line moves faster than it looks.

places.name: Lester's Deli
places.note: Quieter neighbourhood deli beloved by locals who avoid the queue.

places.name: Snowdon Deli
places.note: Family-run since 1946, with the full Jewish deli menu beyond the sandwich.

food.name: Tourtiere
food.desc: A Quebecois double-crust meat pie of spiced pork, veal or game, traditionally eaten around Christmas but served year-round in old-school diners.

places.name: La Binerie Mont-Royal
places.note: Tiny 1938 counter serving traditional Quebec home cooking.

places.name: Au Pied de Cochon
places.note: Martin Picard's temple of rich Quebec cooking, foie gras included.

places.name: Marche Jean-Talon
places.note: Market butchers and traiteurs sell tourtiere to take away and reheat.

food.name: Steame hot dog
food.desc: The Quebec casse-croute standard: a steamed bun and wiener with mustard, chopped onion and cabbage, ordered with a side of fries.

places.name: Montreal Pool Room
places.note: Downtown hot dog counter operating in some form since 1912.

places.name: Decarie Hot Dog
places.note: Unchanged 1970s diner locals swear by for steames and poutine.

places.name: Gibeau Orange Julep
places.note: Giant orange roadside landmark for dogs, fries and its frothy drink.

food.name: Portuguese grilled chicken
food.desc: The Plateau's Portuguese community grills piri-piri chicken over charcoal, sold by the half bird with fries, rice and hot sauce.

places.name: Romados
places.note: Rotisserie institution with a permanent line out onto Rachel Street.

places.name: Ma Poule Mouillee
places.note: Charcoal chicken plus the city's best-known Portuguese poutine.

food.name: Quebec craft beer
food.desc: Quebec brews some of North America's most characterful beer, from Belgian-style abbey ales to farmhouse saisons poured in neighbourhood brasseries.

places.name: Dieu du Ciel!
places.note: Legendary brewpub; the Peche Mortel imperial stout made its name.

places.name: Vices & Versa
places.note: All-Quebec tap list of around 30 beers with a leafy back terrace.

places.name: Brasserie Harricana
places.note: Bright neighbourhood brewery with a wide range brewed on site.

food.name: Quebec cider
food.desc: Orchards south of the city make crisp dry ciders and the local speciality cidre de glace, an intense ice cider pressed from frozen apples.

places.name: Marche Jean-Talon
places.note: Producer stalls pour tastings of cider and ice cider from nearby orchards.

places.name: Marche Atwater
places.note: Market shops stocking Quebec ciders alongside cheese and charcuterie.

places.note: Keeps Quebec ciders on tap beside the beer list.

landmarks: Notre-Dame Basilica

This Gothic Revival masterpiece dazzles with a deep blue, star-studded ceiling and intricate wood carvings that rival Europe's grandest cathedrals. Its evening light show, Aura, transforms the interior into a mesmerizing sound-and-color experience.
Mount Royal (Parc du Mont-Royal)

Designed by the same landscape architect as New York's Central Park, this forested hill offers the city's best panoramic skyline views from the Kondiaronk Belvedere. It's a beloved year-round escape for hiking, picnicking, and tobogganing.
Old Port of Montréal (Vieux-Port)
Cobblestone streets lined with 17th-century stone buildings lead down to a lively waterfront with boat tours, street performers, and clock tower views. It's the postcard heart of historic Montréal.
Olympic Stadium (Stade Olympique) and Tower

Built for the 1976 Olympics, this futuristic stadium features the world's tallest inclined tower, with a cable car ride to an observation deck offering sweeping city views. Its bold, saucer-like architecture remains a sci-fi landmark on the skyline.
Jean-Talon Market

One of North America's largest open-air markets bursts with colorful Quebec produce, artisanal cheeses, and maple treats year-round. It's a feast for the senses and a favorite among locals and food-loving visitors alike.
Habitat 67

This radical modular apartment complex, built for Expo 67, looks like a stack of interlocking concrete cubes rising from the riverfront. It remains one of the most photographed and architecturally daring residences in the world.
Saint Joseph's Oratory

Perched on the slopes of Mount Royal, this is Canada's largest church and a major pilgrimage site, crowned by a copper dome visible across the city. Climbing its steps rewards visitors with sweeping views and a serene, monumental interior.
Place Jacques-Cartier

This sloping cobblestone square in Old Montréal buzzes with outdoor cafes, street artists, and horse-drawn carriages beneath a Nelson monument. It's the liveliest gathering spot in the historic district.
Biodome and Botanical Garden

Part of the same Olympic Park complex, these attractions let visitors walk through recreated ecosystems and stroll among one of the world's finest botanical collections, including a stunning Chinese garden. It's a lush, immersive break from the urban core.
Underground City (RÉSO)

A sprawling subterranean network connecting metro stations, shops, and offices, this is the largest underground complex in the world and a fascinating way to explore Montréal during winter. It's less a single sight than an only-in-Montréal experience.

intl.to: New York City (United States) via the Hudson Valley

train.note: The once-daily Adirondack leaves Montreal's Central Station (Gare Centrale) in the morning; US border checks happen near Rouses Point, so carry your passport. The route has suffered repeated seasonal suspensions for Canadian track work in recent summers, so confirm it is running before you plan. VIA Rail trains to Toronto, Ottawa and Quebec City also use Central Station.

bus.note: Cross-border coaches depart from the Gare d'autocars de Montreal (Berri-UQAM); you clear US immigration at the border, so have your passport ready.

ferry.note: No international ferries run from Montreal. Only seasonal local river shuttles and sightseeing boats operate on the St Lawrence (e.g. Navettes Maritimes du Saint-Laurent to Longueuil and the islands).

half.name: Mont-Tremblant
half.blurb: A pretty alpine resort village offering hiking, skiing and lake activities beneath forested Laurentian peaks.

half.name: The Laurentians
half.blurb: This rolling mountain region north of the city brims with lakes, trails and cozy villages.

half.name: Eastern Townships
half.blurb: Gentle countryside of vineyards, orchards and lakes dotted with welcoming small towns and farm stands.

half.name: Omega Park
half.blurb: A sprawling safari park where you drive among bison, elk, wolves and roaming native wildlife.

full.name: Quebec City
full.blurb: This walled colonial city charms with cobbled lanes, historic ramparts and a grand riverside chateau.

full.name: Ottawa
full.blurb: Canada's capital pairs stately parliament buildings with riverside pathways, gardens and a scenic historic canal.
